thread.section_title: Barron's Up and Down Wall Street
thread.title: What’s Eating Elon Musk?

author: Randall W. Forsyth
title: What’s Eating Elon Musk?
text:
Photo: Getty Images By Randall W. Forsyth May 4, 2018 10:24 a.m. ET
It was the conference call replayed around the world. Not since April 2001, when former Enron CEO Jeff Skilling called an analyst an “asshole” for daring to question why the infamous energy-trading firm couldn’t produce a quarterly balance sheet or cash-flow statement, has a CEO’s retort caused such a stir.
Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla (ticker: TSLA), was less crude in cutting off an analyst on the company’s earnings conference call on Wednesday, declaring, “Boring bonehead questions are not cool” before his inquisitor could finish his question. Later, he shut down another analyst, asserting, “These questions are so dry. They’re killing me.” Then he switched from professional analysts to a YouTube platform, where Musk deemed the questions more interesting.
Tesla’s stock market value was marked down by about $2 billion on Thursday, apparently in reaction to what might charitably be described as Musk’s mercurial behavior. More than a few observers subsequently recalled that Enron filed for Chapter 11 several months after Skilling’s outburst. Others defended Musk, saying he was addressing actual Tesla investors, not naysaying short sellers. Those who couldn’t take the volatility shouldn’t own the shares, he declared.
Musk tried to defend blowing off the supposed “bonehead” question, which he said in a tweet on Friday concerned capital expenditures that was already answered in the headline of the earnings report. And, indeed, the release did say capex would be cut from more than $3.4 billion to less than $3 billion in 2018. But a replay of the conference call indicates that the analyst wanted to know about capital requirements, not expenditures. That is, the capital on the company’s balance sheet, rather than plant and equipment.
The need to raise capital—to replace the cash that Tesla is burning at a rapid rate—is at the core of company’s conundrum. Yet that key matter wasn’t addressed directly in the long disquisition about the company’s operations that accompanied the earnings release.
Musk claims that Tesla will ramp up production of its Model 3 sedan to 5,000 units per week from more than 2,000 “for three straight weeks,” and eventually to 10,000. Model 3 output is the key to generating the revenues to stanch Tesla’s cash burn and fulfilling the expectations of the stock bulls.
There is another class of investors who are also interested, a cohort that is becoming more skeptical. These, of course, are Tesla’s bondholders, who see the company’s obligations coming due before the cash flows in sufficient quantities to meet them. Given that Tesla has been loath to issue more equity, even if it would be more prudent, the company may have to address its creditors’ concerns.
Bruce Clark, Moody’s Investors Service’s lead automobile analyst, expects that Tesla will have to raise new capital of about $2 billion—in equity, convertible notes, or straight debt—to meet his estimated cash burn in 2018 and refund $1.3 billion of convertibles that mature in late 2018 and early 2019. Those converts had been issued in the expectation of being exchanged for stock at a significantly higher price than Friday’s $294; instead, the securities will have to be paid off in cash.
Newsletter Sign-up Raising that cash won’t be cheap—certainly not as cheap as the 5.3% five-year notes that Tesla marketed last August. As this column observed at the time, that was a better deal for the company than for the creditors. Since then, the notes have fallen to a price of 88, lifting their yield to 7.47% for the junk-rated notes (cut to Caa1 by Moody’s in March). And their spread over comparable Treasuries—the key measure of the market’s assessment of creditworthiness—has widened markedly, to 4.56 percentage points from 3.2 at time of issue.
The high-yield market has been generous recently in providing E-Z credit to other dicey borrowers, a decision it may be ruing in retrospect, given the subsequent price declines of their bonds. WeWork, whose creative accounting metrics also receives attention in Streetwise and was discussed here last week, saw its bonds fall further, to 95 at week’s end from 97.50 on the previous Friday and par when issued a few days earlier.
Musk often is hailed as the new Steve Jobs, an innovator who can change the world. Apple (AAPL) has become the world’s most valuable stock, mainly because of his vision, with Berkshire Hathaway (BRK.A) scooping up an additional 75 million shares in the first quarter, helping to lift Apple’s stock to a record.
If Tesla does ultimately lead the way to a carbon-free future, the societal impact of the iPhone will be trivial in comparison. Unlike Musk, however, Jobs maintained a bulletproof balance sheet, hoarding cash so he could pursue his vision without financial constraints. For Tesla, issuing equity would dilute current shareholders, which would make it harder for all of Musk’s stock options to vest. But given Tesla stock’s extravagant valuation, it might be a better long-term tack than answering to nettlesome bondholders, who annoyingly want to be paid back with interest.
You may call it a bull , but the stock market has become a cash cow for governments.
The bull market is filling the coffers of federal and state governments, as your 2017 tax checks get cashed. That windfall now is doubtlessly welcome, but it also raises the risk of even bigger deficits if, or more likely when, a bear appears.
Uncle Sam took in 12% more tax revenue this April than he did in that month in 2017, according to an estimate by Strategas’ Washington policy group, led by Dan Clifton. Exclude an additional business day this April and the estimate still shows a hefty 7% gain.
“Driving tax-revenue growth is capital gains from the rising stock market,” Strategas writes. “We believe the tax revenue estimates do not reflect the tax revenue impact from share repurchases, dividends, and [mergers and acquisitions] activity,” it added. Those impacts are almost impossible to forecast, so future tax revenues are likely “to surprise on the upside from current revenue estimates,” the note concluded optimistically.
On the state level, revenues had been growing the past two years at about the rate of inflation, according to a report from Standard & Poor’s, but they would have been rising even slower except for personal income taxes. That category incorporates capital-gains taxes from the bull market.
But S&P sounds a note of caution: “Because it has rested on an appreciating stock market, we believe there is risk built into the current level of state tax revenues, despite the sluggish performance in recent years.”
On the federal level, Strategas sees a strong correlation between shareholder wealth and nonwithheld tax revenue a year later, which is when capital-gains taxes show up. That should offset some of the revenue losses from tax cuts, it adds. Recent M&A activity also should boost future tax revenues.
S&P, meanwhile, notes that the recent surge in volatility serves “as a reminder that each of the past two recessions were associated with sharply declining financial asset prices, which undermined state tax revenues and wreaked havoc with budgets.”
Given spreading teacher protests, S&P notes, those declines would be met with pressures for increased education spending. It also notes that the Trump administration’s infrastructure proposal mainly shifts the public-sector role to states and localities from the federal government.
The states face other budget challenges, especially Medicaid spending, which, S&P points out, is forecast to increase by 66%—or $958 billion—from 2016 to 2025. While the federal government is slated to cover 59% of the increase, S&P worries about the risk if Washington shifts from the current expansionary fiscal policy to austerity. And still-distressed pension systems face challenges, even during this economic expansion.
It isn’t just what’s happening to the Dow Jones Industrial Average that affects states and localities. The Wall Street Journal reported that AllianceBernstein plans to relocate most of its staff to Nashville from New York in a cost-cutting move. It joins other money-management firms looking for cheaper places, including Pimco, which the Journal said plans to open an Austin, Texas, office in addition to its Southern California headquarters. Charles Schwab and Fidelity Investments also have Denver offices.
Connecticut has been the poster child for financial firms—especially hedge funds—fleeing for less-costly areas. Some major banks once had trading floors bigger than football fields in Stamford; those have been closed since the financial crisis. The state has granted millions in subsidies to Bridgewater Associates and AQR Capital Management to expand in the Nutmeg State, rather than join the exodus, which included General Electric moving its headquarters to Boston.
In its most recent ranking of states’ credits, Connecticut ranks 46th out of 50, according to Conning & Co., which bases the tally mainly on economic measures, such as employment, income, and per capita economic output. New Jersey comes in at No. 43, while New York ranks No. 32. So, the wider New York metro area, which Wall Streeters call home, is in the bottom two quintiles of the states—even with the bull market.
Conning also points to an additional pressure on high-tax states such as these: the limitation of the federal state and local tax deduction to $10,000 under the new tax law. That’s a fraction of the property taxes on houses in the pricey suburbs in the New York tri-state area, let alone the income taxes on the high pay needed to live there.
Departures such as AllianceBernstein’s would likely pressure home prices, as well. Conning estimates that Connecticut’s were up less than 4% in the past year, and New Jersey’s, about 4.5%. New York prices rose 6%, according to federal data.
A bull market tends to paper over such problems. Governments might not have a direct stake in the stock market, but still could be losers when the bear returns.
